title: When negative gearing was quarantined in 1985–87, rents rose sharply in Sydney and Perth but not in other capitals
oneLiner: The one time Australia tried this, the rent effect showed up in two cities with tight vacancy and nowhere else.
body: Real rents rose strongly in Sydney and Perth during the quarantine period, which is the episode usually cited as proof that rents would spike. Rents in Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide were flat or fell in real terms over the same period, which suggests local vacancy rates, not the tax change, drove the increases.
contextBackground: Two years of data from forty years ago carry an unusual amount of weight in this debate because they are the only natural experiment available.
contextDisagreement: The city-level figures are agreed. Whether they exonerate the tax change, or merely show it interacted with local conditions, is the dispute.

evidenceItems.citation: Grattan Institute, Hot property (2016) — discussion of the 1985–87 quarantine and capital-city rents
Australian Bureau of Statistics, Consumer Price Index — rents component by capital city, 1985–1988

claimItself.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market
claimItself.oneLiner: Fewer landlords means fewer rentals, and fewer rentals means higher rents.
claimItself.body: If the after-tax return on rental property falls, some investors will sell and fewer will buy. Opponents of reform argue that the resulting withdrawal of rental stock would raise rents for the tenants the policy is meant to help.
